Juneteenth — Juneteenth commemorates the enforcement of emancipation in Texas on 19 June 1865 and is now a US federal holiday.
ANZAC Day — ANZAC Day began as a commemoration of Australian and New Zealand soldiers at Gallipoli and now honours their wider military service and sacrifice.
Day of Reconciliation — The Day of Reconciliation was created in 1995 to acknowledge different South African histories and promote unity after apartheid.
Waitangi Day — Waitangi Day commemorates the first signing of the Treaty of Waitangi, a foundational and contested document in New Zealand history.
The Communist Manifesto — The Communist Manifesto set out a concise account of class struggle and called on workers of all countries to unite.
The Little Red Book — The Little Red Book is the popular name for Quotations from Chairman Mao Tse-tung, one of the most widely printed political books in history.
Letter from Birmingham Jail — Letter from Birmingham Jail argues that people have a moral responsibility to resist unjust laws and explains why waiting for civil rights was unacceptable.
Common Sense — Common Sense attacked monarchy and argued for American independence in language intended for a broad colonial audience.
The Green Book — The Green Book outlined Gaddafi’s claimed alternative to capitalism and communism and became compulsory ideological reading in his Libya.
Iron Lady — “Iron Lady” was the Soviet-coined nickname that became inseparable from Margaret Thatcher’s uncompromising public image.
Madiba — “Madiba,” Mandela’s Thembu clan name, became a widely used respectful form of address for him.
Uncle Ho — Ho Chi Minh was widely known by the affectionate political nickname “Uncle Ho.”
El Comandante — Fidel Castro was widely called “El Comandante,” a title rooted in his leadership of the Cuban Revolution.
Great Helmsman — Mao Zedong was celebrated in official political culture as the “Great Helmsman,” casting him as the guide steering China.
MeToo movement — The MeToo movement grew from Burke’s activism into a global wave of survivor testimony amplified by the #MeToo hashtag.
Kony 2012 — Kony 2012 was Invisible Children’s viral campaign to make Joseph Kony internationally famous and press for his capture.
Bring Back Our Girls — Bring Back Our Girls used the #BringBackOurGirls hashtag to demand the return of the abducted Chibok schoolgirls.
SOPA/PIPA blackout — The SOPA/PIPA blackout was the January 2012 web protest against the Stop Online Piracy Act and PROTECT IP Act.
It Gets Better Project — The It Gets Better Project collected encouraging videos intended to show bullied LGBT young people that life can improve.
Larry — Larry is the resident Downing Street cat whose formal job title is Chief Mouser to the Cabinet Office.
Bo — Bo was the Obama family’s Portuguese Water Dog and one of the best-known White House pets of the 2010s.
Socks — Socks was the Clinton family’s adopted stray and became a highly visible White House cat during Bill Clinton’s presidency.
Pushinka — Pushinka was Strelka’s puppy, sent by Nikita Khrushchev to the Kennedy family during the Cold War.
Checkers — Checkers was the dog Nixon named in his successful televised defence against allegations about campaign funds.
British window tax — The British window tax tied the bill to the number of windows, leaving blocked openings as a visible architectural legacy.
Russian beard tax — Peter the Great’s Russian beard tax made payers carry a token proving they had paid to retain their beards.
Vespasian’s urine tax — Vespasian’s urine tax applied to trade in urine collected from public urinals; the episode is linked to the phrase pecunia non olet, “money does not stink.”
British hat tax — The British hat tax was collected through licences and revenue stamps fixed inside hats, with penalties for forgery.
Mussolini’s bachelor tax — Mussolini’s bachelor tax charged unmarried Italian men as part of the regime’s demographic campaign.
Wellington boot — The Wellington boot developed from footwear commissioned by the Duke of Wellington and later became the familiar waterproof “wellie.”
Nehru jacket — The Nehru jacket is a fitted, hip-length coat with a mandarin collar named after Jawaharlal Nehru.
Churchill cigar — Churchill visited Romeo y Julieta in Havana in 1946, and its seven-inch Julieta No. 2 size became known as a Churchill cigar.
Bismarck herring — Bismarck herring is a named form of pickled herring; the response requires both the political surname and the food.
Eisenhower jacket — The Eisenhower jacket, also called the Ike jacket, was the short wool field jacket associated with General Dwight D. Eisenhower and later made standard issue.
Principality of Sealand — The Principality of Sealand is the micronation Bates proclaimed on Fort Roughs off the English coast.
Republic of Užupis — The Republic of Užupis is Vilnius’s bohemian neighbourhood republic, proclaimed on 1 April with a deliberately whimsical constitution.
Liberland — Liberland is Jedlička’s claimed micronation on the Danube borderland between Croatia and Serbia.
Rose Island — Rose Island was Rosa’s artificial-platform micronation off the Italian coast, later dramatized in a Netflix film of the same name.
Conch Republic — The Conch Republic was Key West’s tongue-in-cheek 1982 secession protest against the Border Patrol checkpoint.
Ceylon — Sri Lanka gained independence as the Dominion of Ceylon, retained Ceylon as its country name, and adopted Sri Lanka on becoming a republic in 1972.
Persia — Persia was the long-established Western exonym for Iran; the 1935 request concerned international usage, not the legal creation of a new state.
Siam — Siam was the internationally familiar name of the country officially renamed Thailand in 1939.
Zaire — Zaire was the Mobutu-era name of the present-day Democratic Republic of the Congo; Kabila restored a Congo-based name in 1997.
Upper Volta — The Republic of Upper Volta became Burkina Faso under Sankara; its former name referred to the upper Volta River basin.
Queen Elizabeth II and Paddington Bear — Queen Elizabeth II and Paddington Bear shared tea and revealed their emergency marmalade sandwiches in the filmed Jubilee sketch.
Elvis Presley and Richard Nixon — Elvis Presley and Richard Nixon met at the White House, where their unexpected handshake was photographed.

assertion: Dennis Rodman and Kim Jong-un — Dennis Rodman and Kim Jong-un formed an unusual connection through Rodman’s North Korea visits and their shared interest in basketball.
Princess Diana and John Travolta — Princess Diana and John Travolta danced at the White House, creating the famous image behind the “Travolta dress” nickname.
Mikhail Gorbachev and Pizza Hut — Mikhail Gorbachev and Pizza Hut came together in a commercial that turned debate about his legacy into a toast over pizza.
